claims.claim: Living at home at 6 months similar with hospital at home vs admission
claims.supporting_passage: At 6-month follow-up, 528 of 672 (78.6%) participants in the CGA HAH group versus 247 of 328 (75.3%) participants in the hospital group were living at home (relative risk [RR], 1.05 [95% CI, 0.95 to 1.15];= 0.36)
claims.pico_timeframe: Stable older people referred for admission / HAH with CGA / hospital admission / living at home / 6 months
claims.safe_wording: About 79 in 100 treated at home and 75 in 100 admitted were living at home six months later; the trial did not show a clear difference.
claims.qualifications: Selected, physiologically stable people, mean age 83, mostly from acute medical assessment units; 2:1 randomisation.

numbers.meaning: living at home at 6 months, 528/672 vs 247/328

claims.claim: Deaths at 6 months similar
claims.pico_timeframe: as above / death / 6 months
claims.safe_wording: About 17 in 100 in each group had died by six months; no clear difference.
claims.qualifications: Wide CI; not powered as equivalence on mortality.

claims.claim: Fewer in long-term residential care at 6 months
claims.supporting_passage: 37 of 646 (5.7%) versus 27 of 311 (8.7%) were in long-term residential care (RR, 0.58 [CI, 0.45 to 0.76];< 0.001)
claims.pico_timeframe: as above / new long-term residential care / 6 months
claims.safe_wording: About 6 in 100 treated at home and 9 in 100 admitted had moved into long-term residential care by six months.
claims.qualifications: Use absolute figures only; the RR 0.58 does not match the crude proportions (adjusted), so do not quote it.

numbers.meaning: in long-term residential care at 6 months, 37/646 vs 27/311

claims.claim: Applicability: selected stable older people
claims.supporting_passage: The findings are most applicable to older persons referred from a hospital short-stay acute medical assessment unit; episodes of delirium may have been undetected.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: The trial included older people who were unwell but stable, mostly referred from short-stay acute medical assessment units; it applies to selected people, not everyone.

claims.claim: Carer outcomes (what hospital at home asks of families)
claims.safe_wording: Do not state any trial finding about carers or carer strain. The post may say, as judgement, that families should ask what help at home involves.
claims.qualifications: Carer data not in abstract; full text/NIHR report not opened.

claims.claim: Pathway halved hospitalisation in nursing home residents with pneumonia
claims.supporting_passage: Thirty-four (10%) of 327 residents in the clinical pathway group were hospitalized compared with 76 (22%) of 353 residents in the usual care group. Adjusting for clustering of residents in nursing homes, the weighted mean reduction in hospitalizations was 12% (95% confidence interval [CI], 5%-18%; P = .001).
claims.pico_timeframe: 680 residents 65+ with lower respiratory tract infection, 22 Ontario nursing homes / on-site pathway / usual care / hospitalisation / trial follow-up 2001-2005
claims.safe_wording: In a Canadian trial, about 10 in 100 residents treated in the home on the pathway went to hospital, against 22 in 100 with usual care.
claims.qualifications: Population was lower respiratory tract infection including pneumonia; Canada, 2001-05; the 12% is a percentage-point difference adjusted for clustering.

claims.claim: No clear difference in deaths, quality of life or function
claims.supporting_passage: The mortality rate was 8% (24 deaths) in the clinical pathway group vs 9% (32 deaths) in the usual care group, with a weighted mean difference of 2.9% (95% CI, -2.0% to 7.9%; P = .23). There were no significant differences between the groups in health-related quality of life or functional status.
claims.pico_timeframe: as above / mortality, HRQoL, function
claims.safe_wording: About 8 in 100 and 9 in 100 died; the trial did not show a clear difference in deaths, quality of life or function.
claims.qualifications: Not powered to show a mortality difference; say 'did not show a clear difference', not 'no effect'.

claims.claim: What the pathway included
claims.supporting_passage: Treatment in nursing homes according to a clinical pathway, which included use of oral antimicrobials, portable chest radiographs, oxygen saturation monitoring, rehydration, and close monitoring by a research nurse, or usual care.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: The home treatment included antibiotic tablets, chest X-rays taken in the home, oxygen level checks, fluids, and close checks by a dedicated research nurse.
claims.qualifications: UK applicability to homes without this monitoring is a judgement and should be framed as such.

claims.claim: Proportion of readmissions judged avoidable varies widely
claims.supporting_passage: The median proportion of readmissions deemed avoidable was 27.1% but varied from 5% to 79%.
claims.pico_timeframe: 34 studies of hospital readmissions, 1966-2010 / case-review judgement / proportion avoidable
claims.safe_wording: Across 34 studies, reviewers judged between 5 and 79 in 100 readmissions avoidable; the middle value was about 27 in 100.
claims.qualifications: Denominator is readmissions, not patients.

numbers.meaning: median proportion of readmissions deemed avoidable across studies

claims.claim: Methods mostly subjective, single centre, one reviewer; true proportion unclear
claims.supporting_passage: Most of the studies were conducted at single teaching hospitals, did not consider information from the community or treating physicians, and used only one reviewer to decide whether readmissions were avoidable. ... All but three of the studies used subjective criteria to determine whether readmissions were avoidable. ... The true proportion of hospital readmissions that are potentially avoidable remains unclear.
claims.pico_timeframe: n/a
claims.safe_wording: Most studies relied on one reviewer's judgement at a single teaching hospital, so the true share of avoidable readmissions remains unclear.
claims.qualifications: Position that a rate should prompt case review is judgement.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Auerbach 2016 not checked; do not cite it.

claims.claim: Discharge planning slightly shortened initial stay for people admitted with a medical condition
claims.supporting_passage: Participants allocated to discharge planning and who were in hospital for a medical condition had a small reduction in the initial hospital length of stay (MD - 0.73, 95% confidence interval (CI) - 1.33 to - 0.12; 11 trials, 2113 participants; moderate-certainty evidence)
claims.pico_timeframe: Inpatients with a medical condition (average age 60 to 84) / individual discharge plan / routine discharge / length of stay
claims.safe_wording: Stays were on average about three quarters of a day shorter (moderate certainty).
claims.qualifications: Medical-condition subgroup, 11 trials.

numbers.meaning: mean difference in initial length of stay

claims.claim: Modestly fewer readmissions over about three months
claims.supporting_passage: and a relative reduction in readmission to hospital over an average of three months follow-up (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.97; 17 trials, 5126 participants; moderate-certainty evidence)
claims.pico_timeframe: as above / readmission / average 3 months
claims.safe_wording: Readmissions over about three months were somewhat lower, roughly a tenth fewer in relative terms (moderate certainty).
claims.qualifications: Relative effect only; control rate not available, so no per-100 figure.

claims.claim: Little or no difference in mortality and function; satisfaction may increase; costs uncertain
claims.supporting_passage: There was little or no difference in participant's health status (mortality at three- to nine-month follow-up: RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.29; 8 trials, 2721 participants; moderate certainty) functional status and psychological health ... low certainty evidence). There was some evidence that satisfaction might be increased ... (very low certainty evidence). The cost of a structured discharge plan compared with routine discharge is uncertain
claims.pico_timeframe: as above
claims.safe_wording: There was little or no difference in deaths or day-to-day function; satisfaction may be higher and costs are uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Certainty low to very low for function and satisfaction.

claims.claim: Medication errors and discrepancies are common after discharge
claims.supporting_passage: For adult patients, the median rate of medication errors and unintentional medication discrepancies following discharge was 53% [interquartile range 33-60.5] (n = 5 studies) and 50% [interquartile range 39-76] (n = 11), respectively.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults discharged to community / errors and discrepancies / follow-up 2-180 days
claims.safe_wording: Studies commonly find medicine errors or unintended differences after leaving hospital; in most studies between a third and three quarters of patients were affected.
claims.qualifications: Few studies (5 and 11), varying definitions; give as a range.

claims.claim: Taking weekly methotrexate daily by mistake can cause serious harm; MHRA measures
claims.supporting_passage: Intoxication with oral low-dose methotrexate (MTX) is a well-known and frequent problem, which is often discovered accidently. The major reason is error in the frequency of dosing, mostly of daily instead of weekly intake.
claims.pico_timeframe: case report
claims.safe_wording: Taking a once-weekly medicine such as methotrexate every day by mistake can cause serious poisoning.
claims.qualifications: Case-report level only; MHRA Drug Safety Update not opened, so do not cite MHRA.

claims.claim: On discharge day the ward may already have given that day's doses, and a weekly medicine's day may change during admission, causing doubled or missed doses at home
claims.safe_wording: No source found; cannot be stated as fact.
claims.qualifications: Central premise of the post.

claims.claim: Rapid discharge home for a person expected to die soon depends on several separate arrangements, and the usual causes of delay are getting home equipment, medicines and discharge documents, and poor communication between teams.
claims.supporting_passage: Process mapping, an Ishikawa diagram and a Pareto chart were used to identify barriers, which included timely acquisition of home equipment and medication and poor communication among stakeholders. | After the team debrief, it was determined that the reasons for the two failed ComD after the third PDSA cycle from May 2022–April 2023 were due to delays in obtaining home equipment and discharge documents. | Delays in obtaining discharge medications were sometimes due to the cumbersome task of filling in manual prescription forms for controlled drugs
claims.location: Abstract (Methods); Results, Outcome, process and balance measures; Results, PDSA cycle 3
claims.pico_timeframe: People in one Singapore hospital expected to die within hours to 7 days and discharged home; QI project May 2020 to April 2023
claims.safe_wording: A hospital improvement project in Singapore found that the usual causes of delay in getting a dying person home were getting equipment and medicines to the house, discharge paperwork, and poor communication between teams.
claims.qualifications: One hospital, no control group. Barriers were identified by a staff team using process mapping and voting, not measured in a trial. Do not say these are 'the main barriers' everywhere. Another batch (C13-B3, PMID:38816007) found similar barriers in an English project; not re-opened here.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found. Applicability to Scottish or other UK hospitals is not tested in this source.

claims.claim: Some people who are referred for rapid discharge to die at home die in hospital before the discharge happens.
claims.supporting_passage: Cases where patients could not go home due to delays were termed 'failed ComD'. | After the first PDSA cycle from May 2020 to April 2021, the ComD success rate was 88.9% (n=16). Postpandemic awareness of ComD increased, with success rates of 94.2% (n=49) after the second PDSA cycle from May 2021 to Apr 2022 and 96.7% (n=59) after the third PDSA cycle from May 2022 to April 2023. Unsuccessful ComD cases were excluded as they were unrelated to the process. | After the team debrief, it was determined that the reasons for the two failed ComD after the third PDSA cycle from May 2022–April 2023 were due to delays in obtaining home equipment and discharge documents. | In the period from May 2022 to April 2023 after PDSA cycle 3, there were 19 unsuccessful ComD cases. Reasons included patient's rapid deterioration despite a smooth process (n=10), family caregiver changing their mind (n=7) and patient being unsuitable for ComD due to medical reasons (n=2). | A failed ComD is when the patient dies in the hospital despite initiating the workflow, with the failure potentially due to the workflow (eg, delays).
claims.location: Methods, Measures; Results, Outcome, process and balance measures; Figure 2 legend
claims.pico_timeframe: One Singapore hospital; people with death expected within hours to 7 days; 12 months after each of three cycles (2020 to 2023)
claims.safe_wording: In one Singapore hospital's improvement project, in the year to April 2023, 59 of 61 rapid discharges got the person home (about 97 in 100); in the other 2 the person died in hospital after delays in equipment and paperwork. A further 19 requests did not go ahead for other reasons, mostly because the person got worse very quickly (10) or the family changed their mind (7).
claims.qualifications: Single hospital in Singapore, quality improvement project, not UK data; no comparison group or pre-project failure rate. The denominator 61 is the number of cases in which the checklist was used (stated in the paper); the 2 of 61 = 3.3% matches the paper's own '3.3%'. No UK source found for how often people die before a rapid discharge happens. Keep wording as 'in one hospital' and do not generalise to a UK rate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Internal inconsistency in the paper: the Measures section ties '2 patients (3.3%) dying in the hospital' to the second cycle, whereas Results tie 2 failed discharges to the third cycle. Use only the third-cycle figures. Whether the 10 who deteriorated died in hospital is not stated; say 'did not get home', not 'died'.

numbers.meaning: successful rapid discharges, May 2022 to April 2023, one Singapore hospital
failed discharges (died in hospital) in that year, due to delays in equipment and documents
requests that did not proceed for reasons unrelated to the workflow: 10 rapid deterioration, 7 family changed mind, 2 medically unsuitable

claims.claim: Starting every step on the same day (equipment, symptom medicines, community nurses, GP, overnight care, transport) gives the best chance of getting home in time.
claims.supporting_passage: ComD activation involves various tasks happening simultaneously. Primary doctors coordinate home palliative care, prescribe medications and discharge documents while managing other acutely ill patients. Pharmacists ensure safe and timely dispensing of opioids. Ward nurses provide caregiver training (CGT) on tasks like injectables and diaper changes, arrange oxygen and transport and communicate discharge instructions. | It is acknowledged that the success rate of ComD cannot be attributed to using the ComD resource package alone.
claims.pico_timeframe: Descriptive account of process in one hospital; not a comparison of parallel versus sequential working
claims.safe_wording: Rapid discharge involves several tasks that happen at the same time (equipment, medicines, paperwork, transport, training for family), and a delay in any one can stop the person getting home. Asking for each to be started at once is a reasonable judgement, but no study found here compared starting all steps together with starting them in turn.
claims.qualifications: The paper describes parallel tasks and a checklist; it does not test same-day starting or a named coordinator. Mark 'start everything the same day, with one named coordinator' as judgement ('We should', 'It makes sense to'), not a finding. Do not write that it 'gives the best chance'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Success cannot be attributed to the package (authors' limitation).

claims.claim: National guidance recommends planning symptom medicines in advance (anticipatory prescribing) for the last days of life.
claims.supporting_passage: This Concise Guideline overviews NICE Clinical Guideline (NG31), which addresses: recognising dying; communication and shared decision making; maintaining hydration; and pharmacological symptom control, including anticipatory prescribing.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults in the last days of life; NICE NG31 (2015)
claims.safe_wording: National NICE guidance on care in the last days of life covers planning symptom medicines in advance, so they are available at home.
claims.qualifications: Abstract of a summary article only; NG31 text not opened. NICE guidance formally applies to England; do not present as Scottish guidance. Do not state which medicines or how many.

claims.claim: In England, NHS Continuing Healthcare Fast Track funds care quickly for people who are rapidly deteriorating and may be entering a terminal phase.
claims.supporting_passage: Search-engine summary only (page not opened): the tool is for people whose condition is rapidly deteriorating and may be entering a terminal phase; it is the version integrated care boards and NHS England should use from 1 July 2022; a completed tool is sufficient on its own to establish eligibility.
claims.pico_timeframe: England, guidance July 2022
claims.safe_wording: Leave out. If the editor insists, say only 'In England, NHS Continuing Healthcare has a fast track route for people who are rapidly worsening', and label it England only.
claims.qualifications: Access is search_extract, which is not enough for an essential claim. Scotland and other UK nations use different arrangements; no source opened for them. The post's same-day principle does not depend on this claim.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Guidance currency after August 2022 not confirmed.

claims.claim: New pressure sores develop during emergency department stays, more often in people over 75; most are early (stage I) and on the heels and sacrum.
claims.supporting_passage: A total of 27 patients developed new PU during their ED stay, among them 20 were aged over 75 years. The cumulative incidence was 4·9% and this rate increased to 15·7% in patients aged over 75 years. | Heels and sacrum were both the main sites of PUs, and new PUs were most often localised on these two sites with a greater tendency to appear on the heels. Stage I PUs were the most often stages registered among the 38 new PUs that occurred during the ED stay [i.e. 34 (89·5%) PUs]. | Length of stay, hours (mean ± SD) 9·1 (8·5) | A proportion of 165 (27·4%) patients were older than 75 years.
claims.pico_timeframe: 602 adults in one French ED, 1 to 15 June 2010; skin examined at admission and discharge by trained nurses; new pressure ulcers (including stage I) during the ED stay; mean stay 9.1 hours
claims.safe_wording: In one French emergency department, about 5 in 100 patients developed a new pressure sore during a stay that averaged 9 hours; among people over 75 it was about 16 in 100. Most were stage I, the earliest stage (reddened skin that is still unbroken), mostly on the heels and the base of the spine.
claims.qualifications: One centre, two weeks in 2010; stage I included; 361 of 963 patients excluded for missing data. The incidence denominators appear to be patients without a sore on arrival (overall 602 minus 47 = 555 gives 27/555 = 4.9%; over-75s 165 minus 38 = 127 gives 20/127 = 15.7%): this is the checker's arithmetic, not a statement in the paper. 20 of 165 over-75s would be 12%, so do not compute any other percentage. Say 'in one French emergency department'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Stay longer than 4 hours was linked with new sores only before adjustment (92.6% of those with new sores versus 67.5% without, P = 0.014); after adjustment length of stay was not independent (OR 1.5, 95% CI 0.3 to 7.5, P = 0.618), whereas more long-term conditions (OR 1.3) and higher CRP (OR 1.005) were. So the study does not show that longer waits independently raise the risk; the abstract's wording that a short stay is 'sufficient to induce' sores is causal and must not be repeated. The study did not test repositioning or any preventive measure.

numbers.meaning: cumulative incidence of new pressure ulcers during ED stay, all patients without a sore on arrival
patients with new ulcers who were over 75
new ulcers that were stage I

claims.claim: Older people are more likely than younger adults to have long emergency department stays.
claims.supporting_passage: Attendances of adults aged 65 to 74 years, 75 to 84 years and ≥ 85 years, respectively, had an increased risk (odds ratio (95% confidence interval) of length of ED stay ≥ 4 h of 1.52 (1.45-1.58), 1.65 (1.58-1.72), and 1.84 (1.75-1.93), compared to those of adults 18 to 64 years (all p < 0.001). | Table 3 (stay ≥ 4 h, all attendances): Aged 18 to 64 years 45,311 (43.6); 65 to 74 years 9,027 (63.1); 75 to 84 years 11,156 (71.4); ≥ 85 years 10,142 (79.0)
claims.pico_timeframe: 146,636 adult attendances, one English ED, 2019; stay of 4 hours or more; odds ratios adjusted for socio-demographic and clinical factors including triage acuity
claims.safe_wording: At one large English emergency department in 2019, about 44 in 100 visits by adults aged 18 to 64 lasted 4 hours or more, compared with about 71 in 100 visits by people aged 75 to 84 and about 79 in 100 by people aged 85 or over.
claims.qualifications: One hospital, one year; counts visits (a person can attend more than once), not people; 4 hours is the cut-off, so it says nothing about 12-hour waits. Percentages are the crude figures; the adjusted odds ratios should not be turned into 'times more likely'.

numbers.meaning: visits with ED stay of 4 hours or more, ages 18-64 / 65-74 / 75-84 / 85+, Nottingham 2019

claims.claim: Usual medicines can be given late or missed in hospital, and for time-critical medicines such as Parkinson's drugs this is linked with harm.
claims.supporting_passage: Richard 2022: Time-critical medications were prescribed correctly on admission in 50% of admissions, with errors in medication timing most common (31.6%). Of all doses, 51.7% were administered >30 minutes late, and 29.7% of doses were administered >1 hour late. | Lertxundi 2017: Medication errors, affecting almost one third of admissions and half of patients, were associated with higher mortality: inappropriately omitted dopaminergic drug doses OR = 1.92 CI 95% (1.34-2.76). Inappropriately omitted doses and both inappropriate antipsychotic and antiemetic administration were associated with a significant 4-day increase in median hospital stay.
claims.pico_timeframe: People with Parkinson's disease admitted to hospital (Dublin 15 months; Basque Country 2011-2012); dose timing/omission; length of stay and in-hospital mortality
claims.safe_wording: For some medicines, such as Parkinson's drugs, timing matters. In one Dublin hospital, about half of Parkinson's doses were given more than 30 minutes late. In Spanish hospitals, missed Parkinson's doses were linked with longer stays and more deaths in hospital.
claims.qualifications: Inpatient wards, not emergency department waits; Parkinson's only; observational (link, not proof). The sources do not cover medicines in general, and the NPSA 2010 report on omitted and delayed medicines was not opened, so do not cite it. Ask 'when are my usual medicines due?' as a question without claiming harm from a missed dose for all medicines.

claims.claim: During a long wait an older person still needs a drink (if allowed), help to the toilet, and help to change position, and it is reasonable to ask for each.
claims.supporting_passage: No source opened on dehydration, continence or repositioning during emergency department waits.
claims.safe_wording: Present as a judgement and as questions ('Ask whether they are allowed to drink', 'Ask for help to the toilet', 'Ask whether they can be helped to change position'). Make no claim that any of these prevents harm in the emergency department.
claims.qualifications: The pressure-sore data (C15-15-a) show the risk exists but do not test repositioning.

Central claim C15-04-c (doses already given on discharge day / weekly day shifting causing doubled or missed doses) has no source; MHRA alert not opened. Per editor guidance replace with C15-15. Further PubMed searches (2026-09-25) for last-dose-time information at discharge and for weekly-dosing errors at transfer found no source for the central claim; fallback is C15-15.

Barriers to rapid discharge (equipment, medicines, paperwork, communication) and the fact that a small number of people die in hospital before rapid discharge are supported by one Singapore quality improvement project (full text opened), not by UK data. The claim that starting everything the same day gives the best chance is untested (judgement only). Fast Track is search_extract only and England only. NICE NG31 anticipatory prescribing supported by abstract only.
candidates.revised_angle: Same-day principle for all UK readers framed as judgement: a rapid discharge home to die involves several separate tasks (equipment, medicines for symptoms, paperwork, community nurses, transport), delays in any one can stop it, so ask for each to be started at once and ask who is coordinating. Use the Singapore figures as 'in one hospital' (59 of 61 got home; 2 died in hospital after delays in equipment and paperwork). Leave NHS Continuing Healthcare Fast Track out. Fallback C15-15 if the editor wants UK-sourced numbers.

candidates.reason: Risk context supported (pressure sores in one French ED; older people have longer ED stays in Nottingham), but the stay-length link is not independent after adjustment, medicine-timing evidence is Parkinson's inpatient only, and the four basic-care requests have no source (judgement).
candidates.revised_angle: Keep the four requests as questions framed as judgement. Add one verified fact: in one French emergency department about 5 in 100 patients (about 16 in 100 over 75) developed a new, mostly early, pressure sore in a stay averaging 9 hours; and in Nottingham about 79 in 100 visits by people aged 85 or over lasted 4 hours or more. Do not say longer waits cause sores or that repositioning prevents them. Schedule apart from C15-14.
